# Diagnostics for the primary normalization profile {#sec-normdiag}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run used:** none — these are properties of the normalized scores under
`r norm_profile` (and `initial` for contrast), before any recommendation.
:::

## Raw vs. normalized, AW and SE

E and H are monotone linear rescalings, so only the two logged dimensions are
worth plotting: this is where the long right tail gets compressed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-raw-vs-norm
#| fig-cap: "Raw impact mapped to normalized goodness for the two logged dimensions under the primary profile."
#| fig-height: 4.5
bind_rows(lapply(c("AW", "SE"), function(d) data.frame(
  dimension = d, raw = RAW_IMPACT[[d]], norm = select_mat_primary[, d]))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(raw, norm)) + geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .35) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = paste0("Raw impact to normalized goodness (", norm_profile, ")"),
       subtitle = "log(x + offset) then percentile min-max: the long right tail is compressed",
       x = "raw impact (higher = worse)", y = "normalized goodness (higher = better)")
```

## Normalized scores by category

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplots-by-cat
#| fig-cap: "Normalized scores by L1 category under `initial` (top) and the primary profile (bottom). Watch AW and SE lift off the floor under the log profile."
#| fig-height: 11
#| fig-width: 15
make_dim_boxplot <- function(m, ttl) {
  data.frame(L1 = l1cat, Overall = as.numeric(m %*% ALGO_WEIGHTS),
             E = m[, "E"], AW = m[, "AW"], SE = m[, "SE"], H = m[, "H"]) %>%
    pivot_longer(-L1, names_to = "dimension", values_to = "score") %>% filter(!is.na(score)) %>%
    mutate(dimension = factor(dimension, levels = c("Overall", dim_cols))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(dimension, score, fill = dimension)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = .35, alpha = .85, linewidth = .3) +
    facet_wrap(~ L1) +
    labs(title = paste0("Normalized scores by L1 category - ", ttl), x = NULL,
         y = "normalized score (higher = better)") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6),
          legend.position = "none", strip.text = element_text(size = 6.5))
}
print(make_dim_boxplot(NORM[["initial"]], "initial"))
print(make_dim_boxplot(NORM[[norm_profile]], norm_profile))
```

The layout above groups by category, which is best for comparing dimensions
*within* one category. The version below mirrors @sec-raw's raw-impact
figure instead — one panel per dimension, category on the y-axis — which is
better for comparing one dimension *across* every category at a glance.
Primary profile only, shown on a shared 0-1 axis since (unlike the raw
figure) all four dimensions are already on the same normalized scale, so
there's no need for `free_x`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-norm-boxplots-by-dim
#| fig-cap: "Normalized scores per L1 food category, one panel per dimension, primary profile. Same layout as the raw-impact figure in the raw diagnostics, but all four panels now share the same 0-1 axis since the dimensions are already on a common scale."
#| fig-height: 9
norm_long <- data.frame(L1 = l1cat, select_mat_primary) %>%
  pivot_longer(-L1, names_to = "dimension", values_to = "score") %>% filter(!is.na(score)) %>%
  mutate(dimension = factor(dimension, levels = dim_cols),
         L1 = factor(L1, levels = rev(sort(unique(L1)))))
ggplot(norm_long, aes(score, L1, fill = dimension)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = .35, alpha = .8, linewidth = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = paste0("Normalized scores by L1 category and dimension"), # (", norm_profile, ")"),
       #subtitle = "Shared 0-1 axis across all four panels - directly comparable to each other, unlike the raw-impact version",
       x = "Normalized score (higher = better)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

## Normalized dimension pairs

```{r}
#| label: fig-norm-pairs
#| fig-cap: "All six normalized dimension pairs under the primary profile (goodness scale, higher = better)."
#| fig-height: 7
bind_rows(lapply(prs, function(p) data.frame(
  pair = paste0("x = ", p[1], "   |   y = ", p[2]),
  x = select_mat_primary[, p[1]], y = select_mat_primary[, p[2]]))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point(size = .4, alpha = .25) + facet_wrap(~ pair) +
  labs(title = paste0("Normalized dimension pairs (", norm_profile, ")"),
       x = "x-axis dimension (see facet header)", y = "y-axis dimension (see facet header)")
```

## Quartile grid: what do the other dimensions look like?

Column = the dimension used to split products into quartiles; row = which
quartile. Orange is that dimension's own range; blue is the other three
dimensions and the overall score, **for exactly the same products**. This shows
the trade-off structure as it is actually distributed, rather than as a single
correlation coefficient.

```{r}
#| label: fig-quartile-grid
#| fig-cap: "Dimension trade-offs by quartile under the primary profile."
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 12
ov_q <- as.numeric(select_mat_primary %*% ALGO_WEIGHTS)
bind_rows(lapply(dim_cols, function(ref_d) {
  qs <- factor(dplyr::ntile(select_mat_primary[, ref_d], 4), levels = 1:4,
               labels = c("Q1 (worst 25%)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (best 25%)"))
  bind_rows(lapply(c(dim_cols, "Overall"), function(show_d) data.frame(
    ref_dim = ref_d, quartile = qs, shown = show_d,
    score = if (show_d == "Overall") ov_q else select_mat_primary[, show_d])))
})) %>%
  filter(!is.na(quartile), !is.na(score)) %>%
  mutate(ref_dim = factor(ref_dim, levels = dim_cols),
         shown   = factor(shown, levels = c(dim_cols, "Overall")),
         is_ref  = shown == as.character(ref_dim)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(shown, score, fill = is_ref)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = .3, alpha = .85, linewidth = .3) +
  facet_grid(quartile ~ ref_dim,
             labeller = labeller(ref_dim = function(x) paste0("split on ", x))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#d95f02", `FALSE` = "#7fc7d9"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "the splitting dimension", `FALSE` = "other dimensions"),
                    name = NULL) +
  labs(title = paste0("Dimension trade-offs by quartile (", norm_profile, ")"),
       x = NULL, y = "normalized score (higher = better)") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

# Comparing normalization profiles {#sec-normcompare}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run used:** every profile is put through the same objective-gate algorithm at
level `r substitutability_level`, deterministic best-in-pool, so differences
reflect the normalization and nothing else.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Choosing which profiles to compare.** Quarto renders to static HTML, so a live
"include/exclude" button would need Shiny. The selector is therefore the
`PROFILES_TO_COMPARE` parameter in @sec-parameters — set it to `NULL` for all
profiles, or to e.g. `c("initial", "log_tails", "log_tails_TL")` to restrict.
Where `kableExtra`/`DT` is installed the tables below are also scrollable and
sortable, which covers most of the "hide what I don't need" use case.
:::

```{r}
#| label: profile-selection
PROFILES <- if (is.null(PROFILES_TO_COMPARE)) names(norm_profiles) else
  intersect(PROFILES_TO_COMPARE, names(norm_profiles))
cat("Profiles compared:", paste(PROFILES, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## Correlations between normalized dimensions

Spearman is invariant to any monotone per-dimension transform, so it is
identical for every bounded profile and equal to the raw Spearman from
@sec-raw. It is reported anyway, as requested, because seeing it constant is the
cleanest evidence that the profiles differ in *magnitude* handling and not in
*ordering*. Pearson is what the log actually moves.

```{r}
#| label: profile-correlations
profile_corr <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  m <- NORM[[pn]]
  bind_rows(lapply(prs, function(p) data.frame(
    profile = pn, pair = paste0(p[1], "-", p[2]),
    pearson  = round(cor(m[, p[1]], m[, p[2]], use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 3),
    spearman = round(cor(m[, p[1]], m[, p[2]], method = "spearman",
                         use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 3))))
}))
save_out(profile_corr, "normalized_dimension_correlations_by_profile.csv",
         "Pearson and Spearman correlations between normalized dimensions, per profile.")
profile_corr %>% pivot_wider(names_from = pair, values_from = c(pearson, spearman)) %>%
  show_tbl(caption = "Correlations between normalized dimensions, by profile. The spearman_* block is constant across bounded profiles by construction.")
```

## Skewness of the normalized scores

Raw skewness (@sec-raw) told you which dimensions needed a transform. This is
the same statistic computed *after* each profile's transform, so it shows how
much skew survives. `rank` should read almost exactly 0 on every dimension by
construction (a rank is, up to ties, uniformly distributed). `log_tails` should
show AW and SE much closer to 0 than `initial`, while E and H barely move,
since only AW and SE are logged in that profile.

```{r}
#| label: profile-skewness
profile_skew <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  m <- NORM[[pn]]
  data.frame(profile = pn,
             skew_E  = round(skewness(m[, "E"]),  3), skew_AW = round(skewness(m[, "AW"]), 3),
             skew_SE = round(skewness(m[, "SE"]), 3), skew_H  = round(skewness(m[, "H"]),  3),
             skew_overall = round(skewness(OVERALL_BY_PROFILE[[pn]]), 3), row.names = NULL)
}))
save_out(profile_skew, "normalized_skewness_by_profile.csv",
         "Skewness of each normalized dimension and of the equal-weight overall score, per profile.")
show_tbl(profile_skew, caption = "Skewness of the normalized scores, per profile. Compare to the raw-scale skewness in the raw diagnostics: initial should still show a positive AW/SE tail; log_tails should not; rank should be near 0 everywhere.")
```

### Why these numbers look so different from the raw skewness in @sec-raw

They shouldn't be compared directly — two things change between raw impact and
this table, and only one of them is about the transform actually working.

1. **The sign flips.** Normalization turns "impact" (higher = worse) into
   "goodness" (higher = better). Skewness of `-X` is exactly `-1` times the
   skewness of `X`, so the sign of every number above is expected to be the
   mirror image of the raw table, regardless of what the transform did.
   `zscore` makes this exact: it only centres and rescales (which never
   changes skewness) before flipping the sign, so its skewness here should
   equal *minus* the raw skewness almost exactly. Checked: raw AW skewness is
   10.546 and `zscore`'s is -10.362; raw SE is 5.438 against -5.438 for
   `zscore` — matching to three decimals once you flip the sign.
2. **The percentile clamp trims the tail further.** `minmax_p`/`log_minmax_p`
   clip at the 1st/99th percentile before flipping, which chops off exactly
   the most extreme contributors to the third moment — so the final number is
   usually *smaller in magnitude* than the sign-flip alone would predict, not
   larger. There's no boundary-pile-up inflation here.

Neither of those tells you whether the **log step itself** reduced the skew,
which is the actual question a log transform is supposed to answer. To check
that in a way that's directly comparable to @sec-raw (same sign, same units,
before either the sign flip or the percentile clamp), the next table measures
skewness right after `log(raw + offset)` — for dimensions a profile doesn't
log, this is identical to the raw-skewness table, since there's nothing else
to measure before the rescale.

```{r}
#| label: profile-skewness-prerescale
# Skewness measured right after the log step (if the profile has one) and
# BEFORE the percentile min-max / clamp / sign-flip. Same sign convention as
# @sec-raw (higher = worse), so this is the number directly comparable to it -
# it isolates "did logging fix the skew" from the two cosmetic effects above.
pre_rescale_skew <- function(raw, method) {
  if (method == "log_minmax_p") {
    o <- if (LOG_OFFSET_MODE == "relative_median") LOG_OFFSET_VALUE * median(raw[raw > 0], na.rm = TRUE)
         else LOG_OFFSET_VALUE
    return(skewness(log(pmax(raw, 0) + o)))
  }
  skewness(raw)   # minmax_p, minmax_whisker, zscore, rank: nothing happens before the rescale step
}

profile_skew_prerescale <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  p <- norm_profiles[[pn]]
  data.frame(profile = pn,
             skew_E  = round(pre_rescale_skew(RAW_IMPACT$E,  p$E),  3),
             skew_AW = round(pre_rescale_skew(RAW_IMPACT$AW, p$AW), 3),
             skew_SE = round(pre_rescale_skew(RAW_IMPACT$SE, p$SE), 3),
             skew_H  = if (p$H == "letters") NA_real_ else round(pre_rescale_skew(RAW_IMPACT$H, p$H), 3),
             row.names = NULL)
}))
save_out(profile_skew_prerescale, "normalized_skewness_prerescale_by_profile.csv",
         "Skewness right after the log step and before the percentile min-max/clamp/sign-flip - directly comparable to the raw-impact skewness in the raw diagnostics.")
show_tbl(profile_skew_prerescale, caption = "Skewness comparable to the raw-impact table: same sign convention, measured before the rescale step. skew_H is NA for profiles using the discrete Nutri-Score letter mapping, since skewness of a 5-level ordinal variable isn't comparable to a continuous one.")
```

This is where the log transform's actual effect on AW and SE shows up: raw AW
skewness is **10.546**; after `log(raw + offset)` it drops to **1.716** (an
84% reduction). Raw SE skewness is **5.438**, dropping to **1.947** (64%) after
the same treatment. That is the real diagnostic for "did logging work" — the
final flipped-and-clamped table above is answering a related but different
question (how skewed is the score the algorithm actually uses), and both are
legitimate, they just aren't the same measurement.

## Distribution shift across profiles

The tables above summarise *where* each profile puts its mean and its spread;
this shows the actual shape. `initial` is the un-logged baseline, `log_tails` is
the primary profile, `rank` is the fully de-skewed extreme — together they
bracket the range of behaviour the other profiles fall between.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of each normalized dimension (and the equal-weight overall score) under three profiles. All three are on the same 0-1 goodness scale, so the panels are directly comparable."
#| fig-height: 13
#| fig-width: 8
dist_profiles <- c("initial", "log_tails", "rank")
dist_long <- bind_rows(lapply(intersect(dist_profiles, names(NORM)), function(pn) {
  bind_rows(
    as.data.frame(NORM[[pn]]) %>% mutate(profile = pn) %>%
      pivot_longer(all_of(dim_cols), names_to = "dimension", values_to = "score"),
    data.frame(profile = pn, dimension = "Overall", score = OVERALL_BY_PROFILE[[pn]]))
})) %>% mutate(dimension = factor(dimension, levels = c(dim_cols, "Overall")),
              profile = factor(profile, levels = dist_profiles))

ggplot(dist_long, aes(score, colour = profile, fill = profile)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .15, linewidth = .7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Normalized-score distributions: initial vs. log_tails vs. rank",
       x = "normalized goodness (higher = better)", y = "density") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This is also the picture behind the "why does almost nothing move under
log_tails" question in @sec-beforeafter: watch the AW panel above — under
`log_tails` roughly half the catalogue is bunched at the very top of the scale
(the zero-AW-impact plant products), while under `rank` the same dimension is
close to uniform across the whole range by construction.
:::

## Signal retention, spread, and magnitude preservation

Three complementary questions about what a normalization keeps:

* **Signal retention** ($\eta^2$): how much of the variance in normalized
  goodness still distinguishes one subcategory from another. Higher = the
  transform did not squash categories together.
* **Spread and `spread_CV`**: the standard deviation of subcategory means per
  dimension, and the coefficient of variation across the four. `spread_CV` near
  0 means each dimension gets an equal say under equal weights; high means some
  dimensions are effectively muted.
* **Gap structure**: does the normalized distance between two subcategories track
  their *linear* raw distance or their *multiplicative* (log) one? AW and SE come
  from multiplicative source methodologies (PAALA is a product of factors, PSILCA
  characterisation factors are powers of ten), so for those two the log profiles
  should track the log gap better. E and H are additive constructs, so linear
  min-max should track the linear gap at least as well.

```{r}
#| label: profile-retention
norm_diag <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  m <- NORM[[pn]]
  sub_sd <- sapply(dim_cols, function(d) sd(tapply(m[, d], subcat, mean, na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE))
  osens <- sapply(dim_cols, function(d) {
    meth <- norm_profiles[[pn]][[d]]
    if (meth == "letters") return(0)
    cn <- paste0(d, "_SS"); base <- norm_one_dim(DB[[cn]], meth, l1cat)
    x2 <- DB[[cn]]; x2[which.max(x2)] <- NA
    mean(abs(base - norm_one_dim(x2, meth, l1cat)), na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  data.frame(profile = pn,
             sd_E = round(sub_sd["E"], 3), sd_AW = round(sub_sd["AW"], 3),
             sd_SE = round(sub_sd["SE"], 3), sd_H = round(sub_sd["H"], 3),
             spread_CV = round(sd(sub_sd) / mean(sub_sd), 3),
             outlier_sens = round(mean(osens), 4),
             eta2_E  = round(eta_sq(m[, "E"],  subcat), 3),
             eta2_AW = round(eta_sq(m[, "AW"], subcat), 3),
             eta2_SE = round(eta_sq(m[, "SE"], subcat), 3),
             eta2_H  = round(eta_sq(m[, "H"],  subcat), 3), row.names = NULL)
}))
save_out(norm_diag, "normalization_spread_and_signal_retention.csv",
         "Per profile: subcategory-level spread per dimension, cross-dimension homogeneity, outlier sensitivity, and eta-squared signal retention.")
show_tbl(norm_diag, caption = "Spread, cross-dimension homogeneity (spread_CV) and between-category signal retention (eta^2).")
```

```{r}
#| label: profile-gap-structure
gap_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  m <- NORM[[pn]]
  bind_rows(lapply(dim_cols, function(d) {
    raw <- tapply(RAW_IMPACT[[d]], subcat, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    g   <- tapply(m[, d], subcat, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    ok  <- !is.na(raw) & !is.na(g); raw <- raw[ok]; g <- g[ok]
    o   <- 0.01 * max(raw[raw > 0], na.rm = TRUE)
    ij  <- combn(length(raw), 2)
    ng  <- abs(g[ij[1, ]] - g[ij[2, ]])
    data.frame(profile = pn, dimension = d,
      r_with_linear_gap = round(suppressWarnings(cor(ng,
        abs(raw[ij[1, ]] - raw[ij[2, ]]), method = "spearman")), 3),
      r_with_log_gap = round(suppressWarnings(cor(ng,
        abs(log(raw[ij[1, ]] + o) - log(raw[ij[2, ]] + o)), method = "spearman")), 3))
  }))
}))
save_out(gap_tbl, "gap_structure_preservation.csv",
         "Spearman of the normalized subcategory gap against the linear and the log raw gap, per profile x dimension.")
gap_tbl %>% pivot_wider(names_from = dimension,
                        values_from = c(r_with_linear_gap, r_with_log_gap)) %>%
  show_tbl(caption = "Gap-structure preservation. For AW and SE the chosen profile should track the log gap more closely than the linear one.")
```

## Construct validity on known pairs

Does the normalized gap between two products you have a strong prior about look
sensible, or does it just echo an accident of raw units? The sign should be
stable across profiles; the *size* is what discriminates them.

```{r}
#| label: construct-validity
find_th <- function(code) { i <- which(DB$TH_code == code); if (!length(i)) NA_integer_ else i[1] }
domain_pairs <- list(
  list(dim = "E",  a = "TH1533", b = "TH1705", note = "E: beef vs chicken"),
  list(dim = "AW", a = "TH1705", b = "TH1533", note = "AW: chicken vs beef"),
  list(dim = "SE", a = "TH1404", b = "TH1401", note = "SE: cashew vs almond"))
cv_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(domain_pairs, function(dp) {
  ia <- find_th(dp$a); ib <- find_th(dp$b)
  if (is.na(ia) || is.na(ib)) return(NULL)
  cbind(data.frame(pair = dp$note, a = DB$food_product[ia], b = DB$food_product[ib]),
        as.data.frame(lapply(setNames(PROFILES, PROFILES), function(pn)
          round(NORM[[pn]][ia, dp$dim] - NORM[[pn]][ib, dp$dim], 3))))
}))
save_out(cv_tbl, "construct_validity_pairs.csv",
         "Normalized goodness gap (a - b) on known product pairs, per profile.")
show_tbl(cv_tbl, caption = "Construct validity: normalized gap (a - b). Positive = 'a' is the more sustainable of the two on that dimension.")
```

## Where the aggregate variance comes from

```{r}
#| label: agg-variance-share
agg_share <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  m <- NORM[[pn]]; ov <- OVERALL_BY_PROFILE[[pn]]; vov <- var(ov, na.rm = TRUE)
  s <- sapply(seq_len(4), function(k)
    ALGO_WEIGHTS[k] * cov(m[, k], ov, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") / vov)
  data.frame(profile = pn, E = round(s[1], 3), AW = round(s[2], 3),
             SE = round(s[3], 3), H = round(s[4], 3))
}))
save_out(agg_share, "aggregate_variance_share.csv",
         "Share of the equal-weight overall score's variance driven by each dimension, per profile (rows sum to 1).")
show_tbl(agg_share, caption = "Share of aggregate-score variance driven by each dimension. Rows sum to 1; equal shares mean equal weights really do give equal influence.")
```

```{r}
#| label: dim-vs-overall
dim_vs_overall <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  m <- NORM[[pn]]
  bind_rows(lapply(names(weight_archetypes), function(an) {
    ov <- as.numeric(m %*% weight_archetypes[[an]])
    data.frame(profile = pn, archetype = an,
      as.data.frame(as.list(setNames(round(sapply(dim_cols, function(d)
        cor(m[, d], ov, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")), 3), paste0("pearson_", dim_cols)))),
      as.data.frame(as.list(setNames(round(sapply(dim_cols, function(d)
        cor(m[, d], ov, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")), 3),
        paste0("spearman_", dim_cols)))))
  }))
}))
save_out(dim_vs_overall, "dimension_vs_overall_correlation.csv",
         "Correlation of each normalized dimension with the overall score, per profile x weight archetype.")
show_tbl(dim_vs_overall, caption = "Correlation of each dimension with the overall score, per profile and weight archetype. For 'AW-heavy', AW should top its own row; where it does not, another dimension is dominating the aggregate regardless of the stated weights.")
```

## Tailoring, per profile

Same construction as @sec-tailoring-theory but with the small systematic sweep
(vary one dimension's weight, split the rest equally) so it stays cheap across
eight profiles. Gate and pool are that profile's own objective equal-weight
score; only the selection is swept.

```{r}
#| label: tailoring-per-profile
WEIGHT_SWEEP_GRID <- seq(0.05, 0.85, by = 0.10)
tailoring_per_profile <- cached(
  paste0("tailoring_per_profile_", LKEY, "_n", length(WEIGHT_SWEEP_GRID), "_", POOL_MODE),
  c(names(norm_profiles), substitutability_level, WEIGHT_SWEEP_GRID, POOL_MODE,
    GATE_THRESHOLD, LOG_OFFSET_MODE, LOG_OFFSET_VALUE, GATE_MODE), {
  cmp <- compat_by_level[[LKEY]]
  bind_rows(lapply(names(norm_profiles), function(pn) {
    m <- NORM[[pn]]
    e <- build_eligibility(OVERALL_BY_PROFILE[[pn]], cmp, ref_cat_vec,
                           GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, POOL_MODE, dim_mat = m)
    srv <- which(e$served)
    td <- sapply(dim_cols, function(d) {
      Wd <- t(sapply(WEIGHT_SWEEP_GRID, function(wd) {
        w <- setNames(rep((1 - wd) / 3, 4), dim_cols); w[d] <- wd; w[dim_cols] }))
      A <- pick_alternatives(e, m, Wd, randomize = FALSE)[srv, , drop = FALSE]
      gains <- colMeans(matrix(m[A, d], nrow(A), ncol(A)) - m[srv, d], na.rm = TRUE)
      suppressWarnings(cor(WEIGHT_SWEEP_GRID, gains, method = "spearman"))
    })
    data.frame(profile = pn, tail_E = round(td["E"], 3), tail_AW = round(td["AW"], 3),
               tail_SE = round(td["SE"], 3), tail_H = round(td["H"], 3),
               tail_min = round(min(td, na.rm = TRUE), 3), row.names = NULL)
  }))
})
show_tbl(tailoring_per_profile[tailoring_per_profile$profile %in% PROFILES, ],
         caption = "Per-profile tailoring: Spearman between the weight on d and the mean gain delivered on d.")
```

## Head-to-head

One table to answer "should I change normalization?". Look for a profile that
lifts AW/SE tailoring without destabilising E/H, without collapsing coverage,
and with a reasonable `spread_CV`.

```{r}
#| label: head-to-head
algo_compare <- bind_rows(lapply(PROFILES, function(pn) {
  a <- run_algo(OVERALL_BY_PROFILE[[pn]], compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, randomize = FALSE)
  ng <- sum(a$gated)
  data.frame(profile = pn, bounded_0_1 = !(pn %in% c("zscore")),
             pct_gated = round(100 * mean(a$gated), 1),
             pct_no_alternative = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "no_alternative"), 1),
             pct_gated_served = round(100 * sum(a$alt_reason == "recommended") / max(ng, 1), 1),
             mean_gain = round(mean(a$gain[a$alt_reason == "recommended"]), 3),
             distinct_alts = length(unique(a$alt_row_id[a$alt_reason == "recommended"])))
}))

norm_head_to_head <- algo_compare %>%
  left_join(norm_diag[, c("profile", "spread_CV", "outlier_sens",
                          "eta2_E", "eta2_AW", "eta2_SE", "eta2_H")], by = "profile") %>%
  left_join(agg_share %>% rename_with(~ paste0("aggshare_", .x), all_of(dim_cols)), by = "profile") %>%
  left_join(tailoring_per_profile, by = "profile")
save_out(norm_head_to_head, "normalization_head_to_head.csv",
         "Consolidated normalization comparison: algorithm behaviour, spread, signal retention, variance share and tailoring in one table.")
show_tbl(norm_head_to_head, caption = "Consolidated normalization head-to-head. zscore is unbounded, so its 0.75 gate is not on the same footing as the bounded profiles.")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Why `rank` is not a candidate despite scoring well here.** Rank normalization
is population-dependent: a score describes a product's position in *this*
database rather than an absolute sustainability property, which makes the 0.75
gate meaningless as a standard and makes every result non-transferable to a
different catalogue. It also destroys magnitude — the roughly 39-fold raw
difference between cashew and lentil on the socio-economic dimension collapses
to a percentile gap of about 0.036.
:::

# Parameter and design-choice sweeps {#sec-sweeps}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run used:** each subsection re-runs the algorithm while varying exactly one
parameter, at level `r substitutability_level` under the primary profile,
deterministic unless stated. **Weight source varies by subsection** — most of
this section deliberately isolates one parameter at a time using a single
weight vector, so a shift in outcome can only be attributed to that parameter:

| Subsection | Weight source |
|---|---|
| Gate threshold | equal weights (single vector) |
| Pool threshold, pool mode | equal weights (single vector) |
| Sharpness | equal weights, repeated 30 times (randomization only, not weight variation) |
| Log offset | equal weights (single vector) |
| Gate definition (overall vs. all-dimensions) | equal weights (single vector) |
| Substitutability level | **the full 1,771-weight grid** (as requested) |
| Objective floor vs. full personalization | 5 archetypes + 60 random draws from the grid |

If you want any of the equal-weight-only subsections repeated across the full
grid instead, the pattern to copy is the substitutability-level subsection
below — it is the one place in this section already built that way.
:::

## Gate threshold {#sec-gate-sweep}

The gate decides *who* gets a recommendation. Raising it serves more people but
the extra people pulled in were already doing fine, so their individual gain is
small. What matters for impact is the product of the two: `total_improvement`,
the sum of gains over all served products.

```{r}
#| label: gate-sweep
GATE_GRID <- seq(0.50, 0.95, by = 0.05)
gate_sweep <- bind_rows(lapply(GATE_GRID, function(gt) {
  a <- run_algo(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                gt, POOL_THRESHOLD, randomize = FALSE)
  g <- a$gain[a$alt_reason == "recommended"]
  data.frame(gate_threshold = gt,
             pct_gated = round(100 * mean(a$gated), 1),
             pct_recommended = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "recommended"), 1),
             pct_no_alternative = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "no_alternative"), 1),
             mean_gain = round(mean(g, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
             median_gain = round(median(g, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
             total_improvement = round(sum(g, na.rm = TRUE), 1))
}))
save_out(gate_sweep, "sweep_gate_threshold.csv", "Gate-threshold sweep including total catalogue-wide improvement.")
show_tbl(gate_sweep, caption = "Gate threshold sweep.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gate-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Coverage rises and per-swap gain falls as the gate rises; total_improvement is their product and typically peaks at an interior value. That peak is the empirically motivated gate, as opposed to the hand-chosen 0.75."
#| fig-height: 4
gate_sweep %>% select(gate_threshold, pct_recommended, mean_gain, total_improvement) %>%
  pivot_longer(-gate_threshold, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(gate_threshold, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c7fb8") + geom_point(size = 1.6, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = GATE_THRESHOLD, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Gate threshold sweep", subtitle = "dashed line = the gate currently in use",
       x = "gate threshold", y = NULL)
```

## Pool threshold and pool mode

```{r}
#| label: pool-sweep
pool_sweep <- bind_rows(lapply(c(0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90), function(pt) {
  a <- run_algo(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                GATE_THRESHOLD, pt, randomize = FALSE, pool_mode = "absolute")
  ng <- sum(a$gated)
  data.frame(pool_threshold = pt,
             pct_gated_served = round(100 * sum(a$alt_reason == "recommended") / max(ng, 1), 1),
             pct_no_alternative = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "no_alternative"), 1),
             mean_gain = round(mean(a$gain[a$alt_reason == "recommended"]), 3))
}))
save_out(pool_sweep, "sweep_pool_threshold.csv", "Pool-threshold sweep under POOL_MODE = absolute.")
show_tbl(pool_sweep, caption = "Pool-threshold sweep (deterministic best-pick, POOL_MODE = 'absolute'). mean_gain is nearly flat because the single best candidate in a pool of dozens is usually well above 0.75 anyway; the threshold mostly changes pool size, not the winner.")
```

```{r}
#| label: pool-mode
pool_mode_cmp <- bind_rows(lapply(c("absolute", "beat_reference", "none"), function(pm) {
  e <- build_eligibility(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                         GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, pm)
  a <- run_algo(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, randomize = TRUE, seed = RANDOM_SEED,
                sharpness = SHARPNESS, pool_mode = pm, elig = e)
  srv <- a$alt_reason == "recommended"
  data.frame(pool_mode = pm,
             pct_no_alternative = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "no_alternative"), 1),
             pct_recommended = round(100 * mean(srv), 1),
             mean_gain_randomized = round(mean(a$gain[srv], na.rm = TRUE), 3),
             n_worse_than_ref = sum(a$gain[srv] < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             pct_worse_than_ref = round(100 * mean(a$gain[srv] < 0, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
             distinct_alts = length(unique(a$alt_row_id[srv])))
}))
save_out(pool_mode_cmp, "sweep_pool_mode.csv", "Comparison of the three pool-eligibility modes.")
show_tbl(pool_mode_cmp, caption = "Pool mode comparison. pct_worse_than_ref is the decisive column: under 'none', softmax makes a downgrade unlikely but not impossible, whereas 'beat_reference' drops the arbitrary 0.75 constant and still guarantees zero downgrades.")
```

## Sharpness

How the randomized draw actually behaves across repeated visits — the real user
experience, which neither the single randomized run nor the deterministic
validation code shows.

```{r}
#| label: sharpness-mc
N_MC <- 30
sharpness_grid <- c(0, 5, 15, 30, 60)
mc_validation <- cached(
  paste0("mc_", norm_profile, "_", LKEY, "_N", N_MC),
  c(norm_profile, substitutability_level, N_MC, sharpness_grid, RANDOM_SEED, POOL_MODE, GATE_MODE), {
  e <- ELIG[[LKEY]]; srv <- which(e$served)
  Wrep <- matrix(rep(ALGO_WEIGHTS, each = N_MC), nrow = N_MC)   # same weights, N_MC draws
  best <- vapply(srv, function(i) e$cand[[i]][which.max(overall_primary[e$cand[[i]]])], integer(1))
  bind_rows(lapply(sharpness_grid, function(sh) {
    A <- pick_alternatives(e, select_mat_primary, Wrep, randomize = TRUE,
                           seed = RANDOM_SEED, sharpness = sh)[srv, , drop = FALSE]
    data.frame(sharpness = sh,
      mean_distinct_alts = round(mean(apply(A, 1, function(r) length(unique(r)))), 2),
      mean_entropy_bits  = round(mean(apply(A, 1, function(r) {
        p <- table(r) / length(r); -sum(p * log2(p)) })), 3),
      mean_realized_gain = round(mean(rowMeans(
        matrix(overall_primary[A], nrow(A), ncol(A)) - overall_primary[srv])), 3),
      pct_draws_is_best  = round(100 * mean(A == best), 1))
  }))
})
save_out(mc_validation, "sweep_sharpness.csv", "Monte Carlo behaviour of the randomized pick across sharpness levels.")
show_tbl(mc_validation, caption = paste0("Sharpness sweep, ", N_MC, " draws per product. Sharpness 0 is a uniform draw (most variety, lowest realized gain); as sharpness rises, realized gain climbs toward the deterministic ceiling while variety falls. This is the variety-vs-quality trade-off made explicit."))
```

## Log offset

```{r}
#| label: offset-sweep
median_nonzero <- function(x) median(x[x > 0], na.rm = TRUE)
aw_med <- median_nonzero(RAW_IMPACT$AW); se_med <- median_nonzero(RAW_IMPACT$SE)
offset_grid <- list(
  list(kind = "absolute", val = 1,     label = "absolute_1"),
  list(kind = "absolute", val = 0.1,   label = "absolute_0.1"),
  list(kind = "relative", val = 0.001, label = "relative_0.1pct_median"),
  list(kind = "relative", val = 0.01,  label = "relative_1pct_median"),
  list(kind = "relative", val = 0.05,  label = "relative_5pct_median"),
  list(kind = "relative", val = 0.10,  label = "relative_10pct_median"),
  list(kind = "relative", val = 1.00,  label = "relative_100pct_median (current)"))
log_at <- function(x, kind, val, med) log(pmax(x, 0) + if (kind == "relative") val * med else val)
minmax_p_of <- function(x, p_lo = .01, p_hi = .99) {
  lo <- as.numeric(quantile(x, p_lo, na.rm = TRUE)); hi <- as.numeric(quantile(x, p_hi, na.rm = TRUE))
  1 - pmin(pmax((x - lo) / (hi - lo), 0), 1)
}
e_fixed <- norm_one_dim(DB$E_SS, norm_profiles[[norm_profile]]$E, l1cat)
h_fixed <- if (norm_profiles[[norm_profile]]$H == "letters") DB$H_letter_goodness else
  norm_one_dim(DB$H_SS, norm_profiles[[norm_profile]]$H, l1cat)

offset_sens <- bind_rows(lapply(offset_grid, function(og) {
  o_aw <- if (og$kind == "relative") og$val * aw_med else og$val
  o_se <- if (og$kind == "relative") og$val * se_med else og$val
  aw_g <- minmax_p_of(log_at(RAW_IMPACT$AW, og$kind, og$val, aw_med))
  se_g <- minmax_p_of(log_at(RAW_IMPACT$SE, og$kind, og$val, se_med))
  m  <- cbind(E = e_fixed, AW = aw_g, SE = se_g, H = h_fixed)
  ov <- as.numeric(m %*% ALGO_WEIGHTS)
  a  <- run_algo(ov, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec, GATE_THRESHOLD,
                 POOL_THRESHOLD, randomize = FALSE)
  rec <- a[a$alt_reason == "recommended", ]
  ia <- find_th("TH1705"); ib <- find_th("TH1533")
  data.frame(offset = og$label,
    pct_of_AW_median = round(100 * o_aw / aw_med, 2),
    pct_of_SE_median = round(100 * o_se / se_med, 2),
    eta2_AW = round(eta_sq(aw_g, subcat), 3), eta2_SE = round(eta_sq(se_g, subcat), 3),
    aggshare_AW = round(ALGO_WEIGHTS[2] * cov(m[, "AW"], ov, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") /
                          var(ov, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    cv_AW_chicken_vs_beef = if (is.na(ia) || is.na(ib)) NA_real_ else round(aw_g[ia] - aw_g[ib], 3),
    pct_gated = round(100 * mean(a$gated), 1),
    top1_share_recommended = round(100 * max(table(rec$alt_TH_code)) / nrow(rec), 1))
}))
save_out(offset_sens, "sweep_log_offset.csv",
         "Log-offset sensitivity at both the normalization and the algorithm level.")
show_tbl(offset_sens, caption = "Log-offset sensitivity. The two 'absolute' rows should differ sharply between pct_of_AW_median and pct_of_SE_median: that asymmetry is the reason to prefer a relative offset. Watch aggshare_AW and top1_share_recommended move together - a smaller offset that raises AW's variance share also concentrates recommendations on fewer products.")
```

## Gate definition: overall score vs. all-dimensions {#sec-gatemode}

`GATE_MODE` (set in @sec-parameters) controls what "good enough, no
recommendation needed" means. This compares the two options head-to-head,
independent of whatever `GATE_MODE` is currently set to for the rest of the
document, at equal weights, level `r substitutability_level`:

* **`overall`** (the default used everywhere else in this document): good
  enough if the equal-weight average of the four dimensions clears
  `r GATE_THRESHOLD`.
* **`all_dimensions`**: good enough only if *every one* of E, AW, SE, H
  individually clears `r GATE_THRESHOLD`. A product that is excellent on three
  dimensions but weak on the fourth no longer escapes attention by averaging
  its way over the bar.

```{r}
#| label: gate-mode-comparison
gate_mode_cmp <- bind_rows(lapply(c("overall", "all_dimensions"), function(gm) {
  e <- build_eligibility(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                         GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, POOL_MODE,
                         dim_mat = select_mat_primary, gate_mode = gm)
  a <- run_algo(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[LKEY]], ref_cat_vec,
                GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, randomize = FALSE, elig = e)
  g <- a$gain[a$alt_reason == "recommended"]
  data.frame(gate_mode = gm,
             pct_gated = round(100 * mean(e$gated), 1),
             pct_good_enough = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "good_enough"), 1),
             pct_recommended = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "recommended"), 1),
             pct_no_alternative = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == "no_alternative"), 1),
             mean_gain = round(mean(g, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
             total_improvement = round(sum(g, na.rm = TRUE), 1))
}))
save_out(gate_mode_cmp, "sweep_gate_mode.csv",
         "Overall-score gate vs. all-dimensions gate, same equal weights and level.")
show_tbl(gate_mode_cmp, caption = "Gate definition comparison. all_dimensions gates strictly more products (a superset of what overall gates), so pct_gated only rises.")
```

```{r}
#| label: gate-mode-hidden-weakness
# The interesting case: products that are "good enough" under overall (their
# average clears the gate) but would be gated under all_dimensions (at least
# one dimension does not). These are exactly the products the overall-score
# gate is silently accepting despite a weak dimension.
hidden_weak <- which(overall_primary >= GATE_THRESHOLD &
                     apply(select_mat_primary, 1, function(r) anyNA(r) || any(r < GATE_THRESHOLD)))
hidden_weak_tbl <- data.frame(
  TH_code = DB$TH_code[hidden_weak], food_product = DB$food_product[hidden_weak],
  SAFAD_L2_cat = ref_cat_vec[hidden_weak], overall = round(overall_primary[hidden_weak], 3),
  E = round(select_mat_primary[hidden_weak, "E"], 2), AW = round(select_mat_primary[hidden_weak, "AW"], 2),
  SE = round(select_mat_primary[hidden_weak, "SE"], 2), H = round(select_mat_primary[hidden_weak, "H"], 2),
  weakest_dim = dim_cols[apply(select_mat_primary[hidden_weak, , drop = FALSE], 1, which.min)])
save_out(hidden_weak_tbl, "gate_mode_hidden_weakness_products.csv",
         "Products that clear the overall-score gate (average >= 0.75) despite at least one individual dimension below 0.75.")
cat(sprintf("%d products (%.1f%% of the catalogue) clear the overall gate despite a weak dimension - these are only caught by the all_dimensions gate.\n",
            length(hidden_weak), 100 * length(hidden_weak) / n_all))
table(hidden_weak_tbl$weakest_dim) %>% as.data.frame() %>%
  setNames(c("weakest_dimension", "n_products")) %>% arrange(desc(n_products)) %>%
  show_tbl(caption = "Which dimension is the one dragging these otherwise-good-enough products down.")
```

The `all_dimensions` gate is strictly more cautious by construction — every
product it gates, `overall` also gates, plus this extra set — so
`total_improvement` rising under `all_dimensions` mixes two effects: more
coverage (mechanically larger) and whether the newly-caught products are worth
catching. The hidden-weakness table above answers the second part directly:
these are real products with a real single-dimension problem the averaged gate
was masking, not an artifact of the comparison.

## Substitutability level

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run used:** the full 1,771-weight grid (`GRID`), all three levels, primary
profile — as requested, rather than equal weights alone. Coverage
(`pct_recommended`, `pct_gated`) itself does **not** need re-deriving here: it
is identical for every weight vector at a given level, since the gate and pool
are objective (see @sec-runs's "Algorithm behaviour by substitutability level"
table). What genuinely varies with the weight vector — and is therefore worth
running on the full grid — is *which* alternative gets picked, how similar it
is to the reference, and how much it improves each dimension.
:::

### How similar are the alternatives actually chosen?

`matrix_A` codes range 0-5; a level-L pool only ever admits codes in `{L,...,5}`.
This tabulates, among alternatives **actually selected** across every served
product and every one of the 1,771 weight vectors, how that admitted range gets
used in practice — not just what the pool allows, but what the softmax-weighted
selection actually picks.

```{r}
#| label: subst-composition

## ========================================================================== #
## 9.x  Substitutability-level composition and impact, on the 1,771 grid ====
## ========================================================================== #
matrix_A_num <- as.matrix(matrix_A); storage.mode(matrix_A_num) <- "numeric"

# code_of(alt_row_id_matrix, ref_L2_vector): matrix_A code between each chosen
# alternative and its (fixed, per-row) reference category. matrix_A is indexed
# [candidate_category, reference_category] (see compat_by_level in @sec-engine).
code_of <- function(alt_mat, ref_L2) {
  alt_L2  <- matrix(DB$SAFAD_L2_cat[alt_mat], nrow(alt_mat), ncol(alt_mat))
  alt_idx <- matrix(match(alt_L2, rownames(matrix_A_num)), nrow(alt_mat), ncol(alt_mat))
  ref_idx <- matrix(match(ref_L2, colnames(matrix_A_num)), nrow(alt_mat), ncol(alt_mat))
  matrix(matrix_A_num[cbind(as.vector(alt_idx), as.vector(ref_idx))], nrow(alt_mat), ncol(alt_mat))
}

subst_composition <- bind_rows(lapply(SUBST_LEVELS, function(L) {
  key <- paste0("L", L); srv <- GRID$served[[key]]; A <- GRID$alt[[key]]
  codes <- code_of(A, ref_cat_vec[srv])
  tab <- table(factor(as.vector(codes), levels = 3:5))
  data.frame(main_level = L, pct_code_3 = 100*tab["3"]/sum(tab),
             pct_code_4 = 100*tab["4"]/sum(tab), pct_code_5 = 100*tab["5"]/sum(tab),
             n_recommendations = sum(tab), row.names = NULL)
})) %>% mutate(across(starts_with("pct_code"), ~ round(.x, 2)))
save_out(subst_composition, "substitutability_composition_by_level.csv",
         "Among all (served product x weight vector) recommendations on the 1,771 grid, the matrix_A code actually realised, by main substitutability level.")
show_tbl(subst_composition, caption = "Composition of CHOSEN alternatives by their true matrix_A code. Impossible cells (e.g. code 3 at main_level 5) are exactly 0, confirming the pool restriction is respected.")
```

```{r}
#| label: subst-pool-composition
# Secondary view: the MENU rather than the pick -- what the eligible pool looks
# like before selection, per category (unweighted by how many products sit in
# that category, unlike the table above which is naturally product-weighted).
pool_composition <- bind_rows(lapply(SUBST_LEVELS, function(L) {
  cmp <- compat_by_level[[paste0("L", L)]]
  codes <- unlist(lapply(names(cmp), function(cc) {
    cand_L2 <- DB$SAFAD_L2_cat[cmp[[cc]]]
    matrix_A_num[match(cand_L2, rownames(matrix_A_num)), match(cc, colnames(matrix_A_num))]
  }))
  tab <- table(factor(codes, levels = 3:5))
  data.frame(main_level = L, pct_code_3 = 100*tab["3"]/sum(tab),
             pct_code_4 = 100*tab["4"]/sum(tab), pct_code_5 = 100*tab["5"]/sum(tab), row.names = NULL)
})) %>% mutate(across(starts_with("pct_code"), ~ round(.x, 2)))
save_out(pool_composition, "substitutability_pool_composition_by_level.csv",
         "Composition of the ELIGIBLE POOL (menu) by matrix_A code, per category, by main level - contrast with the chosen-alternative composition above.")
show_tbl(pool_composition, caption = "Composition of the eligible POOL rather than the pick (one entry per category x candidate, not weighted by product count). Compare to the table above: if the pick's code-5 share exceeds the pool's, the algorithm is gravitating toward closer substitutes even when looser ones are available.")
```

### Average improvement by level, per dimension

Pooled across every served product and all 1,771 weight vectors.

```{r}
#| label: gain-by-level
gain_by_level <- bind_rows(lapply(SUBST_LEVELS, function(L) {
  key <- paste0("L", L); srv <- GRID$served[[key]]; A <- GRID$alt[[key]]
  per_dim <- sapply(dim_cols, function(d) {
    nd <- select_mat_primary[, d]; mean(matrix(nd[A], nrow(A), ncol(A)) - nd[srv])
  })
  ov_gain <- mean(matrix(overall_primary[A], nrow(A), ncol(A)) - overall_primary[srv])
  data.frame(level = L, E = per_dim["E"], AW = per_dim["AW"], SE = per_dim["SE"],
             H = per_dim["H"], Overall = ov_gain, n_served = length(srv),
             n_cells = length(A), row.names = NULL)
})) %>% mutate(across(c(E, AW, SE, H, Overall), ~ round(.x, 3)))
save_out(gain_by_level, "gain_by_substitutability_level.csv",
         "Mean normalized gain per dimension and overall, by main substitutability level, over the 1,771-weight grid.")
show_tbl(gain_by_level, caption = "Mean gain by substitutability level, per dimension and overall, over the full weight grid.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gain-by-level
#| fig-cap: "Mean gain by dimension, grouped by substitutability level. Looser substitutability (level 3) has strictly more room to find a bigger improvement; the question is how much of that room actually gets used."
#| fig-height: 4.5
gain_by_level %>% select(level, E, AW, SE, H) %>%
  pivot_longer(-level, names_to = "dimension", values_to = "gain") %>%
  mutate(dimension = factor(dimension, levels = dim_cols), level = factor(level)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(dimension, gain, fill = level)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .75), width = .65) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "substitutability\nlevel") +
  labs(title = "Mean gain by dimension, by substitutability level", x = NULL, y = "mean normalized gain")
```

### Variety by level

```{r}
#| label: distinct-by-level
distinct_by_level <- bind_rows(lapply(SUBST_LEVELS, function(L) {
  A <- GRID$alt[[paste0("L", L)]]
  data.frame(level = L,
             mean_distinct_alts = round(mean(apply(A, 1, function(r) length(unique(r)))), 2),
             pct_single_alt_always = round(100 * mean(apply(A, 1, function(r) length(unique(r)) == 1)), 1),
             median_top_alt_share_pct = round(100 * median(apply(A, 1, function(r) max(table(r)) / length(r))), 1))
}))
save_out(distinct_by_level, "distinct_alternatives_by_level.csv",
         "Variety of alternatives shown across the 1,771-weight grid, by substitutability level.")
show_tbl(distinct_by_level, caption = "Variety by level. A looser pool (level 3) gives the softmax more distinct products to draw from, which should show up as higher mean_distinct_alts and a lower top-alternative share.")
```

### Putting it together

```{r}
#| label: subst-level-master
pool_size <- bind_rows(lapply(SUBST_LEVELS, function(L) {
  s <- lengths(compat_by_level[[paste0("L", L)]])
  data.frame(level = L, median_pool_size = as.integer(median(s)))
}))
subst_master <- pool_size %>%
  left_join(subst_composition %>% rename(level = main_level), by = "level") %>%
  left_join(gain_by_level %>% select(level, Overall, mean_gain_AW = AW), by = "level") %>%
  left_join(distinct_by_level, by = "level")
save_out(subst_master, "substitutability_level_master_comparison.csv",
         "Consolidated substitutability-level comparison: pool size, chosen-alternative composition, gains, and variety.")
show_tbl(subst_master, caption = "Consolidated view. The trade-off worth reading off this row-by-row: does a bigger median_pool_size at looser levels translate into materially higher Overall/mean_gain_AW and mean_distinct_alts, or mostly into a lower pct_code_5 (less similar swaps) for little extra gain?")
```

```{r}
#| label: level-agreement
det_by_level <- setNames(lapply(SUBST_LEVELS, function(L)
  run_algo(overall_primary, compat_by_level[[paste0("L", L)]], ref_cat_vec,
           GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, randomize = FALSE,
           elig = ELIG[[paste0("L", L)]])), paste0("L", SUBST_LEVELS))
cross_level <- bind_rows(lapply(combn(SUBST_LEVELS, 2, simplify = FALSE), function(pr) {
  a <- det_by_level[[paste0("L", pr[1])]]; b <- det_by_level[[paste0("L", pr[2])]]
  both <- a$alt_reason == "recommended" & b$alt_reason == "recommended"
  data.frame(levels = paste0("L", pr[1], " vs L", pr[2]),
             pct_same_reason = round(100 * mean(a$alt_reason == b$alt_reason), 1),
             pct_same_alternative_if_both_served =
               round(100 * mean((a$alt_row_id == b$alt_row_id)[both]), 1),
             n_both_served = sum(both))
}))
save_out(cross_level, "sweep_substitutability_level.csv", "Cross-level agreement of recommendations (equal weights, deterministic).")
show_tbl(cross_level, caption = "Cross-level agreement, equal weights. Lower agreement between distant levels is expected: a broader pool (L3) can offer a better alternative that a strict pool (L5) simply does not contain.")
```

## Objective floor vs. full personalization {#sec-personalization}

This is the comparison that replaces v11's "pool pre-filter leak" table. That
table reported how far the personalized pool diverges from the objective pool
(Jaccard 0.67–0.80), but as you pointed out, divergence alone says nothing about
whether the divergent picks are any *good*. So the Jaccard is kept here as one
column among several, and the decisive columns are the last two.

The two modes:

* **objective floor** (this document's default): gate and pool on the objective
  equal-weight score; the personal weights only re-rank the survivors.
* **full personalization** (v11's default in its sections 6–7): gate, pool and
  selection all on the personal score.

```{r}
#| label: personalization-comparison
N_PERSONALIZATION_COMPARE <- 60   # random grid vectors, on top of the 5 archetypes

pers_cmp <- cached(
  paste0("pers_cmp_", norm_profile, "_", LKEY, "_n", N_PERSONALIZATION_COMPARE),
  c(norm_profile, substitutability_level, N_PERSONALIZATION_COMPARE, POOL_MODE,
    GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, RANDOM_SEED, GATE_MODE), {
  set.seed(RANDOM_SEED)
  Wtest <- rbind(do.call(rbind, weight_archetypes),
                 GRID$W[sample(nrow(GRID$W), N_PERSONALIZATION_COMPARE), , drop = FALSE])
  rownames(Wtest) <- c(names(weight_archetypes),
                       paste0("grid_", seq_len(N_PERSONALIZATION_COMPARE)))
  cmp <- compat_by_level[[LKEY]]
  e_obj <- ELIG[[LKEY]]

  bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(Wtest)), function(k) {
    w  <- Wtest[k, ]
    ps <- as.numeric(select_mat_primary %*% w)         # this consumer's own score

    # --- mode A: objective floor, personalized selection ---------------------
    altA <- pick_alternatives(e_obj, select_mat_primary, matrix(w, nrow = 1),
                              randomize = FALSE)[, 1]
    # --- mode B: full personalization ----------------------------------------
    e_per <- build_eligibility(ps, cmp, ref_cat_vec, GATE_THRESHOLD, POOL_THRESHOLD, POOL_MODE,
                              dim_mat = select_mat_primary)
    altB  <- pick_alternatives(e_per, select_mat_primary, matrix(w, nrow = 1),
                               randomize = FALSE)[, 1]

    sA <- e_obj$served; sB <- e_per$served
    pool_j <- mean(vapply(which(sA | sB), function(i)
      jacc(e_obj$cand[[i]], e_per$cand[[i]]), numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE)

    data.frame(
      weights = rownames(Wtest)[k],
      is_archetype = k <= length(weight_archetypes),
      mean_pool_jaccard = round(pool_j, 3),
      pct_served_objective = round(100 * mean(sA), 1),
      pct_served_personalized = round(100 * mean(sB), 1),
      pct_same_pick = round(100 * mean(altA[sA & sB] == altB[sA & sB]), 1),
      personal_gain_objective = round(mean(ps[altA[sA]] - ps[sA]), 4),
      personal_gain_personalized = round(mean(ps[altB[sB]] - ps[sB]), 4),
      objective_gain_objective = round(mean(overall_primary[altA[sA]] - overall_primary[sA]), 4),
      objective_gain_personalized = round(mean(overall_primary[altB[sB]] - overall_primary[sB]), 4),
      pct_alt_objectively_worse_objective =
        round(100 * mean(overall_primary[altA[sA]] < overall_primary[sA]), 2),
      pct_alt_objectively_worse_personalized =
        round(100 * mean(overall_primary[altB[sB]] < overall_primary[sB]), 2))
  }))
})
save_out(pers_cmp, "objective_floor_vs_full_personalization.csv",
         "Per weight vector: coverage, pool overlap, gains and downgrade rate under the objective floor vs full personalization.")

pers_cmp %>% filter(is_archetype) %>% select(-is_archetype) %>%
  show_tbl(caption = "The five weight archetypes under both modes.")

pers_cmp %>% summarise(
  n_weight_vectors = n(),
  `mean pool Jaccard` = round(mean(mean_pool_jaccard), 3),
  `% served (objective)` = round(mean(pct_served_objective), 1),
  `% served (personalized)` = round(mean(pct_served_personalized), 1),
  `% identical pick` = round(mean(pct_same_pick), 1),
  `personal gain (objective)` = round(mean(personal_gain_objective), 4),
  `personal gain (personalized)` = round(mean(personal_gain_personalized), 4),
  `objective gain (objective)` = round(mean(objective_gain_objective), 4),
  `objective gain (personalized)` = round(mean(objective_gain_personalized), 4),
  `% downgrades (objective)` = round(mean(pct_alt_objectively_worse_objective), 2),
  `% downgrades (personalized)` = round(mean(pct_alt_objectively_worse_personalized), 2)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  show_tbl(caption = "Averaged over all tested weight vectors.", digits = 4)
```

**How to read this.** `% downgrades` counts recommendations whose alternative is
*worse than the reference on the objective equal-weight score*. Under the
objective floor this is zero by construction — `POOL_MODE = "beat_reference"` is
applied to the objective score, so no recommendation can ever be an objective
downgrade. Under full personalization the same rule is applied to the *personal*
score, so a product that is better on the dimensions this consumer cares about
can still be worse overall, and the rate is non-zero. That is precisely the
question the Jaccard table could not answer: the divergent pools do contain
different products, and some of those products are objectively worse.

The price of the floor is visible in `personal gain`: full personalization
delivers a slightly higher gain *measured on the consumer's own score*, because
it is optimising exactly that quantity without constraint. The trade is
therefore explicit — a small amount of personal-score gain, in exchange for a
guarantee that no consumer is ever steered to something that is worse by the
shared objective standard, plus identical coverage for everyone.
